_readme: Editor's input to tools/picks/build_heatpumps.py. Slot wording, gate wording, cost ranges with their sources, the do-it-yourself lines, brand exclusions and per-zone locks. A lock replaces a computed pick; give the reason in its 'editorNote'. Re-run the script after any change.

performance.label: Best performance
performance.question: What would you buy if comfort and running cost mattered most?
performance.short: The highest-scoring system for this climate on the certified ratings

diy.label: Best do-it-yourself
diy.question: What can a handy owner install safely, legally and with the warranty intact?
diy.short: Pre-charged lines and a warranty that covers an owner install; no rebate

value.label: Best value
value.question: What gives the most back for the money here?
value.short: The best performer from a budget or mid-priced brand, with the rebates that apply

gatesText: Sold in the country, with warranty terms we have read for that country. Brands whose terms we haven't confirmed yet aren't eligible.
In cold zones, ENERGY STAR's cold-climate designation; in Canada, also NRCan's rebate thresholds (COP of at least 1.8 at −15°C and at least 70% of rated output there).
In very cold zones, at least 80% of rated heat output kept at −15°C (5°F); in the North, 85%.
Like for like: 2 to 4 tons for houses with ducts, 1 to 2 tons for a ductless head, 0.5 to 1 ton for one room.

diy.why: Sold for homeowner installation with pre-charged quick-connect line sets; MrCool's DIY warranty needs no registration and covers installs in the US and Canada.

diyNone.default: No owner-installable system passes the gates for this climate.

us/room/diy.name: Midea window heat pump (PWHP)
us/room/diy.note: No holes in the wall: it sits in a sash window and heats to −13°F. About US$2,800–3,000 through Midea distributors (Fast Company, December 2025).

ca.very-cold-east: Design temperatures here run from −25°C to −29°C, colder than the −15°C point every rating stops at. Ask the installer for the maker’s output at your design temperature, and keep a backup heat source.
ca.prairies: Design temperatures here run from −26°C to −33°C, colder than the −15°C point every rating stops at. Ask the installer for the maker’s output at your design temperature, and keep a backup heat source.
ca.north: At −36°C to −39°C design temperatures every air-source heat pump needs a backup heat source. These picks carry most of the winter and the shoulder seasons; envelope work comes first here.

us.very-cold: Minneapolis design temperatures fall well below the 5°F point every rating stops at. Ask the installer for the maker’s output at your design temperature, and keep a backup heat source.
